entities.summary:
Odon de Châtillon (born c. 1050 in Reims, died April 7, 1101), a French cardinal and diplomat, emerged as a pivotal figure in the late 11th-century Gregorian Reform movement and an instrumental architect of the First Crusade. Elevated to Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia by his probable uncle, Pope Urban II (1088–1099), Odon served as a trusted advisor and papal legate, embodying the papacy's renewed authority during a period of profound ecclesiastical transformation. His career spanned the critical years when the Latin Church solidified its spiritual and temporal power, shaping the political and religious landscape of Western Europe and the Levant.

As Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia, Odon de Châtillon held one of the most prestigious positions within the Roman Curia, frequently acting as the Pope's direct representative. He was a key participant in the Council of Clermont in November 1095, where Pope Urban II famously called for the First Crusade, and Odon played an active role in disseminating the crusading message throughout France as a papal legate. His diplomatic missions extended to various regions, including negotiations with King Philip I of France regarding his controversial marriage, demonstrating his involvement in high-stakes ecclesiastical politics and his commitment to enforcing canon law across the Latin West. He advised Urban II on critical policy decisions and helped manage the nascent stages of the crusader movement.
